title: What Is Humulene? The Woody, Hoppy Cannabis Terpene
h1: Humulene Terpene: Aroma, Sources and What Research Explores
metaDescription: The humulene terpene gives cannabis a woody, hoppy aroma. Learn where it occurs, how it relates to caryophyllene, what research explores and how to find it.

body:
The humulene terpene is the woody, earthy aroma compound that cannabis shares with hops. It's usually a supporting note in a strain's scent, and it usually travels with beta-caryophyllene. Here's what humulene is, where else it occurs and what research does and doesn't show.

## Terpenes in a nutshell

Terpenes are the aromatic compounds that give each cannabis strain its smell and much of its flavor. Plants make them for scent and defense, and many of the same compounds turn up in fruits, herbs and spices. Our guide to [cannabis terpenes](/blog/what-are-cannabis-terpenes/) covers the whole family.

## What the humulene terpene is: a sesquiterpene

What is humulene, chemically? Also called alpha-humulene or alpha-caryophyllene, it's a sesquiterpene, built from three isoprene units, with 15 carbon atoms and the formula C15H24. It is not a monoterpene: lighter terpenes such as [myrcene](/blog/myrcene-terpene/) and [limonene](/blog/limonene-terpene/) have 10 carbons. The class matters because larger, heavier sesquiterpenes tend to evaporate more slowly than monoterpenes.

## Aroma, taste and where humulene occurs

Humulene smells woody and earthy, and its flavor is often described as bitter and hoppy. That's no coincidence: it was first identified as a major component of hop essential oil, and its name comes from the hop plant, Humulus lupulus. A 2024 scientific review found it reported in more than 400 species, including:

- **Hops**, where it's one of the main terpenes.
- **Sage**, the kitchen herb.
- **Ginseng**, where it's among the main aroma compounds of the dried root.
- **Black pepper**, whose essential oil lists it among its major compounds.

## Humulene vs. caryophyllene

Humulene and beta-caryophyllene are isomers: same chemical formula, different arrangement of atoms. In cannabis, the two are made by common enzymes, so they tend to appear together. A 2022 analysis of commercial lab data from six U.S. states found a strong link between their levels, so a strain rich in one usually carries the other. Our [caryophyllene guide](/blog/caryophyllene-terpene/) covers its spicier partner.

## What research explores

Most humulene research has taken place in lab dishes and animals. A 2024 scoping review of 340 studies summed it up:

- **Cell studies** measured its activity in a range of cell types, results that don't automatically carry over to people.
- **Rodent studies** found that humulene given by mouth reduced markers of inflammation, and that injected doses acted on cannabinoid receptors.
- **Human studies** are missing. The review noted an absence of clinical trials.

So humulene effects in people remain unstudied, and popular claims about appetite are unproven. The broader idea that terpenes shape how cannabis feels, known as [the entourage effect](/blog/the-entourage-effect/), is still being tested too.

## Finding humulene on labels and in strains

Michigan requires cannabis labels to show THC and CBD content, but not terpenes. Humulene appears only when a producer lists a terpene profile or shares lab results, often as alpha-humulene. Our guide to [reading a cannabis label](/blog/how-to-read-a-cannabis-label/) explains what's required.

There's no official list of humulene strains. Instead, look for products whose top terpene is caryophyllene, often described as peppery or spicy, since humulene tends to appear in the same breakdown. Trust the lab data over strain lore, and ask our budtenders what a product's listing shows. 21+ only. Please consume responsibly.

faq.a: Woody and earthy, with a flavor often described as bitter and hoppy. In cannabis it's usually a background note rather than the lead, so you're more likely to notice it as part of an earthy or peppery profile alongside beta-caryophyllene.

faq.q: Is humulene the same as caryophyllene?
faq.a: No, but they're close relatives. Humulene, also called alpha-caryophyllene, shares beta-caryophyllene's chemical formula with a different structure. Cannabis makes both with common enzymes, so they tend to appear together; in lab data from six U.S. states, their levels were strongly linked.

There's no good evidence that it does in people. Research on humulene has been done in cells and animals, and a 2024 review of 340 studies noted an absence of clinical trials. Appetite claims, like other health claims about a single terpene, remain unproven.

faq.q: How do I know if a product has humulene?
faq.a: Look for a terpene breakdown. Michigan labels must show THC and CBD content, but terpenes are optional, so humulene appears only when a producer lists it or shares lab results. If beta-caryophyllene sits near the top of the list, humulene is often there too.

review.notes: Medical brief: no shop, menu, deals or rewards links. Humulene is called a sesquiterpene and the copy says it is not a monoterpene. Anti-inflammatory and appetite ideas are reported only as rodent research or unproven claims, never as benefits; the cancer-cell findings in the review are left out. No strain names. Fact-check 2026-10-24: 15 claims checked; Dalavaye 2024 and Smith 2022 full texts (Europe PMC), Cho 2012, Bhatia 2024 and Madeddu 2021 (E-utilities), PubChem CID 5281520 and boiling points, and the 2025 Molecules aroma review opened. Fixed: 'almost always' co-occurrence overstatement; unsupported 'dry, slightly spicy' aroma wording in body, FAQ and takeaway. Sources unchanged (6).
